document.title: Cable from Ambassador Raphel, Islamabad, to Secretary of State, Washington: "Subject: USCINCCENT Visit to Pakistan: The Pak Military on Afghanistan"
document.authors: Ambassador Arnold Raphel, U.S. Embassy Islamabad
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), A New Phase in the Great Game: U.S., Soviets, India, Pakistan vied to shape a new Afghanistan in late 1980s | National Security Archive
document.note: Conversations of Gen. George Crist and Raphel with Gen. Akhtar Abdul Rahman and Gen. Aslam Beg. Pakistani generals discuss unseating Najib, keeping the mujahedin united, delaying refugee returns, and an Islamic republic in Afghanistan joining Pakistan, Turkey and Iran in a bloc. Raphel concludes the Paks feel a new phase has started in the perennial great game.

events.description: Separate meetings of Gen. Crist and Amb. Raphel with Gens. Akhtar Abdul Rahman Khan and Aslam Beg on Soviet intentions in Afghanistan.
Cable sent by Embassy Islamabad reporting the Pakistani generals' views.
Iran sent at least two delegations to meet Hazara leaders; Soviets protested both times.
Gen Crist (USCINCCENT) and Amb Raphel held separate meetings with Gens Akhtar and Beg on Soviet intentions in Afghanistan.
Secret cable from Embassy Islamabad to State reporting Pakistani generals' views on Soviet shift and Afghan outcomes.
Iran sent at least two delegations to meet Hazara leaders; Soviets protested each time.

sources_cited: Meetings of Gen. Crist and Amb. Raphel with Gens. Akhtar and Aslam Beg, 29 May 1988
key_claims: Pakistani generals Akhtar and Aslam Beg expect the Soviets to shift their struggle for Afghanistan by fostering mujahideen discord to bolster Najib.
Soviets are pressing Pakistan to cut off the aid pipeline to the mujahideen.
As a fallback the Soviets may separate and control Afghanistan north of the Hindu Kush.
The generals believe only an Islamic republic in Kabul could prevent bifurcation of Afghanistan.
India shares Soviet opposition to an Islamic government in Kabul but is expected to have little success.
Pakistan envisions an Islamic bloc of Afghanistan, Pakistan, Turkey and Iran to block Soviet expansion.
The Embassy doubts the Pakistanis truly believe Najib can be removed peacefully or that mujahideen will avoid infighting.
